title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a rare form of congestive heart failure (CHF) of unknown etiology. Heart failure in the peripartum period was first described in 1849. In 2000, The National Heart Lung and Blood Institute and The Office of Rare Diseases workshop gave 4 criteria for PPCM, becoming the condition's first case definition. The 4 diagnostic criteria for PPCM are as follows: Cardiac failure in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months of delivery Absence of a determinable etiology for the cardiac failure Absence of demonstrable structural cardiac disease before the last month of pregnancy Echocardiographic evidence of diminished left ventricular systolic function noted by one of the following: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 45%, Motion-mode fractional shortening less than 30% Left ventricular end-diastolic dimension exceeding 2.7 cm/m2

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Introduction
content: In the 2019 European Society of Cardiology position paper, Bauersachs and colleagues characterized PPCM based on 3 key criteria: heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an LVEF below 45%, onset near the end of pregnancy or during the postpartum period, and the absence of any other identifiable cause of heart failure. Notably, left ventricular dilation is not a required feature.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Introduction
content: An expanded definition of PPCM has been proposed to include 2 additional categories: early PPCM, which is diagnosed from the 1st to the 9th month of pregnancy, and late PPCM, which is identified between 6 and 12 months after delivery. This broader framework acknowledges variations in the timing of disease onset and extends beyond the traditional postpartum focus. [1]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Introduction
content: PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion. The incidence and prevalence of this condition vary widely, depending on race and geographic regions. [2] The clinical outcome of PPCM is also diverse, ranging from complete recovery to death.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Etiology
content: The exact etiology of PPCM is unknown. Different hypotheses have been formulated. Potential etiologies include viral myocarditis, nutritional deficiencies, autoimmunity, microchimerism, hemodynamic stresses, vascular dysfunction, hormonal insults, and underlying genetics. [3]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: PPCM affects approximately 1 in 2,000 pregnancies globally, though its incidence differs significantly by region. For example, the incidence varies from 1:100 in parts of Nigeria to 1:20,000 in Japan. In rural Haiti, the incidence of PPCM is 1:300. Patients with severe outcomes are more likely to live in communities with greater social vulnerability. [4] PPCM is more prevalent in Asia and Africa. [5] Data shows that 1 in 837 to 1 in 1,374 deliveries in South Asia is complicated by PPCM. [6] [7] This finding supports possible socioeconomic factors and suggests genetic contributions. In the U.S., the PPCM incidence is 1:4,025 live births, with African American women being 3 to 4 times more likely to develop PPCM than Caucasian women and 7 times more likely than Hispanic women.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Cardiomyopathy causes more than 1/3 of late postpartum pregnancy-related deaths in the U.S. In comparison, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including preeclampsia, contribute to 30% to 50% of these mortality cases. Risk factors for PPCM include multiple gestations, older and younger ages (< 20 and > 35 years), a predisposition to heart failure, and anemia. Preeclampsia is the strongest risk factor for the development of PPCM. The mode of delivery, such as cesarean section, is not associated with an increased risk. The incidence of PPCM has increased in the past few years, mainly due to the advent of new techniques for diagnosing PPCM and greater awareness of the condition. [8]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: When considering the timing of diagnosing PPCM, around 19% of cases are identified in the final month of pregnancy, while the majority—approximately 75%—are detected within the 1st month postpartum. Notably, 45% of these postpartum diagnoses occur during the 1st week after delivery.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: The exact causes of PPCM remain unclear, though several mechanisms have been proposed. Pregnancy induces significant hemodynamic changes, such as increased blood volume, cardiac output, and mass. However, these changes alone do not fully explain the condition. Heart failure typically arises postpartum once hemodynamic stress subsides. While myocarditis has been considered a potential etiology, evidence from biopsies and imaging rarely supports it as the primary cause.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Emerging research supports vascular-hormonal mechanisms as the most plausible etiology. Hormonal imbalances during the peripartum period may trigger PPCM in susceptible patients. Prolactin, a pituitary hormone, may be cleaved to yield abnormal 16-kDa prolactin that can damage cardiac blood vessels, leading to systolic dysfunction. Placental hormones, vascular endothelial growth factor, and soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), which are elevated in preeclampsia and multiple pregnancies, have been implicated in cardiovascular damage and the pathogenesis of PPCM. Elevated levels of other hormones, such as progesterone, plasma brain natriuretic peptide, and activin A, may exacerbate cardiac vulnerability, while protective hormones, like relaxin-2, are often suppressed in patients with the condition. [9] Currently, no specific biomarker is used to diagnose PPCM.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Genetic testing is increasingly recommended and should be considered in most cases of PPCM. Genetics may play a role, with approximately 15% to 20% of PPCM cases linked to variants in genes associated with dilated cardiomyopathy, such as TTN. [10] The TTN gene, located on chromosome 2 (2q31), provides instructions for synthesizing titin, the largest sarcomeric protein in the human body.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Titin is a key structural and functional component of the heart and skeletal muscles. Truncating mutations in the TTN gene, along with hormonal and environmental factors, contribute to the development of PPCM. Additional factors, including inflammation, viral infection, autoimmunity, and selenium deficiency (particularly in regions like Nigeria), may also influence the evolution of the disease. While significant progress has been made, the interplay of genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors in PPCM requires further research to clarify the condition's complex pathogenesis. title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Histopathology
content: The diagnosis of PPCM is based on clinical presentation and echocardiographic findings. A myocardial biopsy is unnecessary. However, when performed in rare cases, histopathology should demonstrate patchy fibrosis, myofiber hypertrophy, degeneration, and necrosis with inflammatory endomyocardial infiltrates. Viral genomes, such as herpesvirus 6, parvovirus B19, and Epstein-Barr virus, are occasionally detected. [21]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Most patients with PPCM present soon after delivery, particularly within the 1st week postpartum. The symptoms, which are typically suggestive of heart failure, include orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. However, these symptoms are also often attributed to normal pregnancy. Consequently, a PPCM diagnosis may be easily missed.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Physical examination findings may include tachycardia, elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pulmonary crackles due to pulmonary edema, a 3rd heart sound (S3), and a displaced apical pulse. In severe cases, patients may present with acute respiratory failure or cardiogenic shock, requiring close monitoring in the intensive care unit. Some of the most common risk factors for the development of PPCM are as follows: Advanced maternal age, though many cases are reported in both young and old extremes of age High parity, with 71% of patients diagnosed with PPCM having had 3 or more prior pregnancies [22] Twin or multiple gestation pregnancy Use of tocolytic therapy, especially at more than 4 weeks age of gestation when it can cause silent ischemia [23] African descent Living in poverty Hypertension and preeclampsia Cocaine use

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: As noted above, patients with PPCM commonly present with heart failure symptoms, including shortness of breath, difficulty breathing while lying flat, elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary rales, and bipedal edema. Diagnosing PPCM requires a high clinical suspicion, as its symptoms often mimic those of normal pregnancy. In some cases, the presentation can be sudden and severe, such as in individuals with cardiogenic shock. Occasionally, patients may present with complications like arrhythmias or thromboembolic events. Most cases (60–90%) occur postpartum, with the highest frequency in the 1st week after delivery, although timing varies by region. In the U.S., Black women are more likely than Caucasian women to present later postpartum, which may contribute to poorer outcomes in this group.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: PPCM is an exclusionary diagnosis. Differential diagnoses include preexisting structural heart conditions, pulmonary edema related to preeclampsia without systolic dysfunction, pulmonary embolism, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, and toxin exposure (eg, alcohol or chemotherapy). The primary diagnostic tool is echocardiography.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: PPCM may be diagnosed on echocardiography based on an LVEF below 45%, end-diastolic diameter greater than 2.7 cm/m2, M-mode fractional shortening of less than 30%, or a combination of these features. This systolic dysfunction occurs without other structural abnormalities. Left ventricular dilatation is common but not universal. Echocardiography is sufficient to differentiate PPCM from other causes of heart failure and typically shows left ventricular dilatation of varying degrees, left ventricular systolic dysfunction, right ventricular and biatrial enlargement, mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension, and intracardiac thrombus. [24]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Other findings, such as sinus tachycardia, interventricular delay, or left bundle branch block on electrocardiography (ECG), are nonspecific. Pulmonary edema is typically seen on chest radiography, along with an enlarged cardiac silhouette or pleural effusions. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) can provide valuable insights into systolic function, ejection fraction, and structural abnormalities. A cardiac biopsy is generally not indicated unless another cause of heart failure is suspected, such as cardiac sarcoidosis or giant cell myocarditis.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: PPCM management primarily follows guidelines for nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy due to the limited number of randomized trials specific to the condition. Treatment is generally supportive, focusing on heart failure symptoms and optimizing volume status. Volume control is typically achieved with diuretics and nitrates, though these agents should be used cautiously during pregnancy to avoid hypotension. β-blockers are safe and routinely used during pregnancy, while hydralazine combined with isosorbide dinitrate serves as an alternative for afterload reduction. Neurohormonal blockade with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), and aldosterone antagonists is contraindicated during pregnancy but becomes appropriate postdelivery. [25]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Novel heart failure medications, such as sacubitril-valsartan and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, show promise in improving outcomes in other forms of heart failure. These medications may be used postpartum, although their safety during pregnancy and lactation remains uncertain. Cardiac resynchronization may be considered when medical therapy alone fails to improve ejection fraction or clinical outcomes. [26]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Recent data suggest that an increase in oxidative stress during the peripartum period enhances the formation of abnormal 16-kDa prolactin, which induces toxic effects on cardiac myocytes. Bromocriptine, a dopamine receptor agonist with prolactin-blocking properties, reduces the effect of 16-kDa prolactin on cardiac myocytes and has been associated with better outcomes in small studies. [27]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Advanced treatments, including mechanical circulatory support and ventricular assist devices, are options for severe cases, though adrenergic support may be harmful. Anticoagulation is often necessary due to the heightened thrombotic risk in PPCM, particularly when the ejection fraction falls below 30% to 35%, or atrial fibrillation is present. Given the potential for cardiac recovery, temporary, wearable defibrillators are preferred over implantable devices for managing ventricular arrhythmias.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Labor and delivery in patients with PPCM require an interprofessional team, including specialists in maternal-fetal medicine, cardiology, anesthesia, and advanced heart failure, especially for hemodynamically unstable patients. Vaginal delivery is generally safe for stable patients, and lactation is usually not contraindicated. Bromocriptine, aimed at reducing prolactin levels, is under investigation for patients with an LVEF below 35%.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Genetic counseling and testing are recommended even without a family history of cardiomyopathy. Variants in genes such as FLNC and DSP may increase the risk of ventricular arrhythmias in PPCM, and conditions like Danon disease or Duchenne muscular dystrophy can present as PPCM. Identifying genetic variants can guide family testing and reduce unnecessary monitoring during pregnancy for unaffected relatives.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Clinical outcomes vary, with most patients showing improvement in LVEF within 6 months, although some may experience delayed or incomplete recovery. Up to 10% of patients require left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation or heart transplantation, with worse survival rates compared to age-matched transplant recipients for other indications. Mortality can reach 20%, particularly in low-income countries. Poor prognostic factors include low LVEF at diagnosis, late presentation, ventricular dilation, right ventricular dysfunction, and delayed gadolinium enhancement on magnetic resonance imaging. Interestingly, PPCM associated with preeclampsia shows better LVEF recovery but higher rates of adverse cardiovascular events.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of PPCM includes the following conditions with overlapping manifestations: Normal physiological effects of pregnancy Takotsubo cardiomyopathy Severe preeclampsia or eclampsia Pulmonary embolism Previously undiagnosed valvular disease, such as rheumatic valve disease Acute pulmonary edema from prolonged tocolysis or preeclampsia Cardiac dysfunction secondary to ischemia or stress cardiomyopathy Cardiac dysfunction secondary to arrhythmia Amniotic fluid embolism syndrome Asthma Pneumonia

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: Heart failure is a leading cause of maternal mortality and morbidity in the U.S., with PPCM accounting for up to 70% of heart failure cases during pregnancy. The development of PPCM has been linked to cardiac angiogenic imbalance caused by cleaved 16kDa prolactin, leading to interest in prolactin inhibitors like bromocriptine for treatment. One systematic review and meta-analysis found that adding bromocriptine to standard guideline-directed medical therapy significantly improved LVEF and increased the likelihood of left ventricular recovery. However, no significant reduction was observed in all-cause mortality between the treatment groups. [28]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: PPCM is a major contributor to maternal mortality in the U.S. and other parts of the world, accounting for approximately 60% of cardiogenic shock cases occurring during pregnancy or the early postpartum period. While over half of affected patients experience recovery of cardiac function, the condition still carries significant morbidity and mortality. Some patients may require advanced interventions, such as LVAD placement or heart transplantation.

content: In the U.S., Black women are twice as likely as White women to experience prolonged cardiac dysfunction. When recovery occurs, it takes twice as long. Mortality rates can reach 20%, with the highest rates observed among Black women in the U.S. and women in less developed regions. The condition can profoundly impact not only affected individuals but also their families and newborns during a critical life stage.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: Long-term outcomes are variable. About 50% of patients improve with standard medical treatment. However, 25% develop chronic heart failure, and the remainder die during the course of the disease. [29] Left ventricular size (>6 cm) and ejection fraction (<30%) at the time of diagnosis are strong predictors of left ventricular recovery. Patients should be advised against future pregnancy if the ejection fraction remains low, as mortality is high in such cases. However, if pregnancy is desired, patients should wait at least 5 years after the ejection fraction has normalized.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Complications
content: Breastfeeding is generally considered safe for women with PPCM. The decision to suppress prolactin, either by using bromocriptine or discontinuing breastfeeding, should balance the potential benefits of suppression with the known advantages of breastfeeding for both mother and child. Breastfeeding is associated with significant benefits, including lower infant mortality, and is recommended by the World Health Organization and the American Academy of Pediatrics for the first 6 months, with continued breastfeeding for up to 2 years.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Complications
content: Counseling for women considering a subsequent pregnancy is challenging, as recurrence of PPCM occurs in 10% to 50% of cases, sometimes with worse outcomes. Although the lack of full recovery of systolic function before another pregnancy is linked to poorer outcomes, it is not a definitive predictor. Counseling should address these risks while considering the patient’s strong desire to expand her family. Close monitoring by an interprofessional team during and after subsequent pregnancies is essential to improve outcomes. The following complications have been associated with PPCM: Progression to severe heart failure Cardiogenic shock Arrhythmias Thromboembolic events such as stroke, transient ischemic attack, and left ventricular apical clots Death, which occurs in 7% to 15% of cases globally

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Complications
content: PPCM is a heart condition that affects young women during late pregnancy or early postpartum. Many patients with this diagnosis desire future pregnancies. While echocardiography is commonly used to assess cardiovascular risks, the most accurate method for evaluating these risks remains uncertain. Other methods for evaluating the risk of subsequent pregnancies in patients with PPCM include resting transthoracic echocardiography, exercise stress echocardiography, and dobutamine stress echocardiography. [30]

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence and patient education play a crucial role in managing PPCM. Early recognition of symptoms, such as fatigue, shortness of breath, and edema, is vital for prompt diagnosis and treatment. Patients should be educated about the risks of PPCM, especially if they have a history of hypertension, preeclampsia, or multiple pregnancies, as these factors may increase the likelihood of developing the condition. Counseling on lifestyle modifications, including proper nutrition and weight management, is essential. Educating patients about the potential for recurrence in future pregnancies and the importance of early prenatal care and regular cardiac monitoring can help manage risks.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: PPCM is a condition that occurs in previously healthy women near the end of pregnancy or shortly after delivery and potentially leads to severe heart failure. Although recovery of heart function occurs in 45% to 50% of cases, the long-term mortality rate remains high at 20%. The incidence of PPCM is rising globally, and its exact cause remains unclear, involving factors like oxidative stress, inflammation, hormonal changes, and genetic mutations.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: The 16-kDa prolactin, a product of oxidative stress, is recognized as the main trigger, damaging cardiomyocytes through microRNA-146a and the NF-κβ pathway. Bromocriptine, which inhibits prolactin, may help, though many cases do not respond, suggesting other underlying mechanisms. Current biomarkers, such as BNP, are not specific, and further research is needed to identify better diagnostic and prognostic molecular indicators.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Ongoing investigations into the disease’s pathophysiology, including microRNA and heat shock proteins, may improve diagnostics, treatment strategies, and outcomes. [31] An interprofessional approach is key, and patients should be closely monitored for complications such as arrhythmias and thromboembolism. While prevention remains elusive, early prenatal care and managing risk factors can help reduce the likelihood of PPCM. Women diagnosed with this condition should be counseled about the risks of recurrence in future pregnancies.

title: Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: An interprofessional approach to PPCM is recommended. The prenatal nurse, obstetrician, and nurse practitioner working in obstetrics must be fully aware of this disorder because of its high morbidity and mortality. Only through a prompt and appropriate referral to an interprofessional team that includes a cardiologist can the mortality be improved. An interprofessional approach should be used to manage moderate-to-severe cases. Despite optimal therapy, the condition still carries a mortality rate of more than 10% to 20%. [32] [33]
